topic: Spain holds its first general strike in 14 years over housing costs ahead of a snap election

sources.title: Spain's first general strike in 14 years brings clashing social and political desires to the fore
sources.text:
Barcelona: Millions of Spain's workers are striking Wednesday to demand that the government remedy the nation's housing crisis less than three weeks before a national election that could catapult the far right to power.
Spain's first general strike in 14 years is expected to cause delays to the widely used public transport system and lead to the slowdown or shuttering of businesses, factories and shops across the eurozone's fourth largest economy.
Between workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards, the groups have very different interests in Wednesday's walkout.
Workers and activists want more government action on housing
---------------------------------------------------------------------
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.
Public anger over housing reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much on rent and can't even dream of homeownership.
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike. They soon won the backing of Spain's two main unions, UGT and CCOO.
The housing activists want several measures, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and protection for renters in the form of automatic renewals of leases.
The UGT and CCOO unions are demanding more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.
The strike's official slogan is "Salaries. Housing. Prices."
Spain's left hopes to put focus back on housing
---------------------------------------------------
The nationwide protests over the eviction of Maricarmen propelled Spain's government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them on the grounds they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded by doubling down politically and called the election on Oct. 5, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition.
But then came a brutal high-speed train collision - Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year. That collision, which killed 69 people, has dominated Spanish news and created a drag on Sanchez's campaign just when he had hoped to build momentum.
The strike, says analyst Oriol Bartomeus, is an opportunity for Sanchez's Socialists and the other parties on the Left that he will need to remain in power.
"The Socialists need for the strike to be a success and for there not to be any violence so that the election campaign can swing back to being about housing, back in the framework of Maricarmen," Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press.
On Thursday, the government will again try to have a reduced interim Parliament ratify the two housing decrees that the full lower chamber rejected last month.
Sanchez posted a long video on social media this week, in which he lauded the prior social policies like the 40-hour work week and national health insurance that were the fruit of the workers' movement and the right to strike.
"It wasn't easy, but they changed Spain," Sanchez said, while warning that right-wing parties would bring austerity and underfunded social services.
Veronica Martinez, spokesperson for Sumar, the junior member of the government, separately said "the Left needs the workers of this country to mobilize. Rights are first won on the streets and then later in the institution."
The right could yet benefit from the strike if it turns ugly
-------------------------------------------------------------
The traditional conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox are against any government intervention in the housing market other than incentivizing construction of new homes.
They also both argue that the unions are playing politics and trying to help Sanchez stay in office, with months of polling showing voters leaning toward the Right.
"This strike is not a general strike; it is an electoral strike," Popular Party spokesperson Miguel Tellado said Tuesday. "It is not against the government in power, but rather against the government to be."
But the right-wing parties, which already have joined forces to govern in some Spanish regions, could benefit from the strike if it descends into street violence, according to Bartomeus.
Strikes can result in hardcore union members pressuring shops and offices into closing. Spain, like other European countries, often has peaceful public protests that radical groups take advantage of to clash with police and destroy property.
"The Popular Party and Vox both want the strike to be a flop and to end in scenes of burning dumpsters and shattered shop windows," Bartomeus said. "That way the next morning they can say, This is chaos and we are coming to establish order.'"

sources.title: 2026 Spanish general election
sources.text:
A general election will be held in Spain on 29 November 2026 to elect the members of the 16th Cortes Generales under the Spanish Constitution of 1978. All 350 seats in the Congress of Deputies will be up for election, as well as 209 of 267 seats in the Senate.
Following the 2023 election, Pedro Sánchez was re-elected as prime minister of Spain and formed a third government—comprising the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and Sumar—with the support of Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for a controversial amnesty law. Tensions with the opposition People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox dominated Sánchez's third term, as well as an unraveling international situation (with the ongoing war in Ukraine, the Gaza genocide, the tariff policy of the second Trump administration, and the 2026 Iran war and its economic impact), economic growth amid a rising cost of living, and a number of corruption probes affecting the government (mainly, the Koldo and Zapatero affairs). Also notable were the alleged mismanagements of a number of environmental disasters by PP-controlled administrations (particularly climate crisis-aggravated environmental disasters such as the 2024 Valencian floods and the 2025 and 2026 wildfires), sexual misconduct allegations affecting various parties and institutions, growing public outrage over the management of public services (particularly following the 2025 Iberian Peninsula blackout, and the 2026 Adamuz and Gelida train accidents), and immigration (with critical points in Torre-Pacheco and Ceuta). While Sánchez admitted to having twice hesitated whether to resign—in April 2024 amid a controversial judicial probe into his wife; then in July 2025 after the resignation of Santos Cerdán as PSOE's organization secretary over the Koldo affair—he voiced his intention to run for a new term as prime minister.
Amid major housing protests in the autumn of 2026 and the parliamentary defeat of his relief plans by PP, Vox and Junts, Sánchez dissolved parliament and called the election for 29 November. The member parties of Sumar (except for Podemos, which had split off in December 2023) launched a new alliance, the Broad Front, with former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau replacing Yolanda Díaz as leading candidate. For the first time since 1977, a major left-wing alliance including the PSOE (Senate of Progress) was formed for the upper chamber, prompting PP and Vox to assess potential forms of electoral cooperation. Together with Vox, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo pledged to carry out sweeping right-wing reforms, including on social issues and constitutional reform. The 2026 Urda train collision on 28 October led most parties but Vox to suspend their campaigns and prompted the resignation of Óscar Puente as minister of Transport and Sustainable Mobility.


== Background ==

The 2023 general election saw Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and his ruling coalition—formed by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and Sumar—re-elected with the support of Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for a controversial amnesty law for those tried and convicted for events linked to the 2017–2018 Catalan crisis and the 2019 protests. This deal sparked widespread protests, some of them violent in the days before Sánchez's investiture, seeing clashes near the PSOE's national headquarters in Madrid and the involvement of far-right groups.
Sánchez's third term was marked by a booming economy and falling unemployment, but also by rising living costs and an affordable housing crisis. During this period, a constitutional reform in 2024 introduced people-first language, and a bipartisan agreement ended the five-year blockade of the judiciary council. Political tensions with the People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox intensified, with the government accusing both of "lawfare", disinformation and harassment campaigns. These tensions peaked in April 2024, when Sánchez briefly considered resigning after a controversial judicial investigation into his wife, Begoña Gómez, over alleged influence peddling and embezzlement accusations brought by the far-right-linked group Manos Limpias (Spanish for "Clean Hands"). The government also dealt with the 2025 Iberian Peninsula blackout, repeated failures in Spain's rail network (especially following the 2026 Adamuz and Gelida train accidents), and the MV Hondius hantavirus outbreak.

On the international stage, Sánchez's government dealt with continued EU support for Ukraine in its war against Russia, the tariff policy of the second Trump administration, and the country's role within NATO amid a debate over the five-percent defense spending hike. Its strong criticism of the Gaza genocide led Spain to recognize Palestine and worsened relations with Israel, sparking pro-Palestinian protests and calls to boycott Israeli participation in international competitions, such as the 2025 Vuelta a España, and Spain's RTVE joining others' bid to withdraw from the Eurovision Song Contest 2026. The 2026 Iran war saw Sánchez and U.S. President Donald Trump clash over the use of joint military bases at Rota and Morón, reviving the "No to war" slogan previously used during the 2003 invasion of Iraq. At the same time, the Spanish government sought to address the war's economic impact by approving a €5-billion relief package.
Several political scandals affected the PSOE government during this period, including the Koldo affair (a kickback-for-contract scheme linked to José Luis Ábalos—a former transport minister—and party official Santos Cerdán), the Zapatero affair (involving the lobbying activity of the former prime minister), and judicial probes into Sánchez's brother (for alleged cronyism) and the Spanish Attorney General, Álvaro García Ortiz (for an alleged data leak). Other probes into alleged irregularities in public procurement affected the SEPI holding company and ADIF (Spain's railway infrastructure manager), leading to arrests and police raids. The PP was also hit by scandals, including several affecting the Madrilenian president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso (an investigation into her partner for alleged tax fraud, forgery and organized crime; the controversial purchase of a luxury penthouse using public funds, and unjustified travel expenses); renewed attention on corruption cases during Rajoy's premiership such as the Montoro and Kitchen affairs (alleged cash-for-favours, influence peddling and deep state networks); as well as a resume padding controversy. Sexual misconduct allegations between 2024 and 2026 shook various parties and institutions and led to multiple resignations and dismissals, with the political backlash often compared to the MeToo movement.

Relations between the PP and Vox remained ambivalent, as the two parties competed electorally while still depending on each other to govern. The alleged mismanagement by PP-controlled administrations—including climate crisis-aggravated environmental disasters, such as the 2024 Valencian floods (seeing Carlos Mazón's resignation as regional president) and major wildfires in August 2025 and July 2026; as well as public outrage over an Andalusian Health Service's mishandling of breast cancer screening—was seen as contributing to Vox’s rise in opinion polls, helped by growing anti-political sentiment, denialism, conspiracist ideation and fake news. These issues and immigration (with high points in the 2024 unaccompanied migrant minors' distribution dispute, the 2025 Torre-Pacheco unrest, and the government's 2026 immigration amnesty) further pushed the PP closer to Vox's agenda, with PP's Alberto Núñez Feijóo embracing Santiago Abascal's nativist "national priority" in exchange of support for regional pacts. Concurrently, Vox purged several high-profile figures as it tried to broaden its appeal among working-class voters.
Changes in the political landscape of Catalonia—with Salvador Illa's Socialists' Party taking over the regional government in 2024 and the rise of the far-right Catalan Alliance—saw Junts withdrawing its support from the Spanish government in October 2025, but it remained uncommitted to support a no-confidence motion to oust Sánchez that would require the agreement of both PP and Vox. Throughout late 2025 and early 2026, the PP tried to capitalize on discontent with Sánchez's government by calling early regional elections in Extremadura and Aragon (together with regularly-scheduled ones in Castile and León and Andalusia), but this strategy backfired as the regional PP branches ended up relying even more on Vox to remain in power, while seeing a rise for regionally-based left-wing parties (such as Chunta Aragonesista and Adelante Andalucía). The political space to the PSOE's left fragmented amid Podemos's split from Sumar in December 2023, and Yolanda Díaz's announcement in February 2026 to not run for re-election, with attempts to reorganize it into a broad front of left-wing parties ahead of the general election still ongoing.
The issues of immigration and housing came to a head in the last few months of the government's tenure, amid the 2026 Ceuta migrant crisis and widespread protests across Spain following the high-profile eviction of an 87-year-old by a real estate company in September 2026. Sánchez's attempt to pass a housing relief package through parliament failed due to Junts's opposition, prompting him to dissolve the chambers and call a snap election for 29 November.


== Overview ==
Under the 1978 Constitution, the Spanish Cortes Generales are conceived as an imperfect bicameral system. The Congress of Deputies holds greater legislative power than the Senate, having the ability to grant or withdraw confidence from a prime minister and to override Senate vetoes by an absolute majority. Nonetheless, the Senate retains a limited number of specific functions—such as ratifying international treaties, authorizing cooperation agreements between autonomous communities, enforcing direct rule, regulating interterritorial compensation funds, and taking part in constitutional amendments and in the appointment of members to the Constitutional Court and the General Council of the Judiciary—which are not subject to override by Congress.


=== Date ===
The term of each chamber of the Cortes Generales—the Congress and the Senate—expired four years from the date of their previous election, unless they were dissolved earlier. The election decree was required to be issued no later than 25 days before the scheduled expiration date of parliament and published on the following day in the Official State Gazette (BOE), with election day taking place 54 days after the decree's publication. The previous election was held on 23 July 2023, which meant that the chambers' terms would have expired on 23 July 2027. The election decree was required to be published in the BOE no later than 29 June 2027, setting the latest possible date for election day on 22 August 2027.

The prime minister had the prerogative to propose the monarch to dissolve both chambers at any given time—either jointly or separately—and call a snap election, provided that no motion of no confidence was in process, no state of emergency was in force and that dissolution did not occur before one year after a previous one. Additionally, both chambers were to be dissolved and a new election called if an investiture process failed to elect a prime minister within a two-month period from the first ballot. Barring this exception, there was no constitutional requirement for simultaneous elections to the Congress and the Senate. Still, as of 2026, there has been no precedent of separate elections taking place under the 1978 Constitution.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez repeatedly voiced his will for the next general election to be held when due in 2027, particularly following corruption allegations in June 2025 that led to the resignation of his party's organization secretary, Santos Cerdán. sources.title: 2026 Spanish housing protests
sources.text:
A series of protests began in Spain following the high-profile eviction on 23 September 2026 of an 87-year-old, María del Carmen "Maricarmen" Abascal, which brought the country's ongoing affordable housing crisis back into the spotlight. Public discontent on the issue of housing had already been building up over a scandal involving the controversial purchase of a luxury penthouse by Madrid premier Isabel Díaz Ayuso and the suicide of an evicted woman in L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, Olga Matute, earlier in September. On 26 September, the protests turned into an organised protest camp at the Puerta del Sol square in Madrid, in an action widely compared to the 15-M Movement in 2011, forcing the Spanish government under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to agree to an emergency relief package including a temporary ban on evictions and stronger protection for tenants amid soaring rents.
Protesters have called for the enforcement of the right to housing, access to affordable housing and increased protection of tenants against landlord abuse and price hikes. While they have been very critical of the housing policies of Spanish administrations—both at the national, regional and local level, and regardless of political affiliation—the protests have met with understanding and sympathy from political parties on the left (such as the ruling Spanish Socialist Workers' Party and Sumar), and with open hostility from the right-wing People's Party and Vox. The latter parties, jointly with Together for Catalonia, blocked the parliamentary ratification of the two decree-laws containing the Spanish government's relief measures on 2 October, further fuelling the protests, which spread to cities across the country amid calls for a general strike in defence of housing rights and against property speculation. The parliamentary defeat of the decrees prompted Sánchez to call a snap general election for 29 November 2026, as well as to re-approve the decrees with enhanced protection measures for tenants and force their ratification through the Congress's interim Permanent Deputation.
On 7 October, Maricarmen died in the hospital to which she was taken upon eviction, with her death sparking more protests and renewed political infighting. The protests and their political impact have been described sometimes as part of the worldwide Gen Z protests.


== Background ==


=== Housing crisis in Spain ===
Housing costs and rental prices had been soaring for many years in Spain, particularly in major urban centers, as wages have not increased to the same extent. Housing construction in the country collapsed following the bursting of the Spanish property bubble in 2008 and the subsequent real estate crisis, but population kept growing in larger city areas (such as Madrid), causing a housing shortage in places where it was needed the most; the proliferation of short-term rents for tourism has been another factor, by significantly reducing long-term rental stock and driving up rent prices.
Recent analyses emphasised structural constraints on Spanish housing supply. In its 2025 annual report, the Bank of Spain described restrictions on housing supply growth as the principal factor behind the current housing access crisis, citing slow land development, low productivity and small firm size in residential construction, higher construction costs, and a shortage of skilled labor. Similarly, the OECD reported that only 345,000 permits for new dwellings were issued in Spain between 2022 and 2024, a period when there were 604,000 net new households. This report identified limited buildable land in high-demand areas, lengthy and uncertain permitting procedures, and poor coordination between different levels of government as key issues. The Bank of Spain warned in June 2026 that 750,000 new homes would be needed to close the gap between newly formed households and the available housing stock.
Housing policy has been a heavily disputed battleground between the Spanish government and regional administrations, which hold primary constitutional powers over urban planning and public housing. The central government adopted a Housing Law in 2023 that allowed regions to declare "stressed residential market zones" (Spanish: zonas tensionadas) to enforce state-backed rent caps, but it failed to ease pressure on the country's housing crisis as most regions ruled by the People's Party (PP) fundamentally resisted or blocked these measures, arguing that price controls hurt the market supply.
According to opinion polls, the issue of housing has emerged as one of Spain's major problems since 2025, with those surveyed also frequently showing support for increased government intervention to lower rents. Large demonstrations in support of housing rights and against property speculation took place in October 2024 in Madrid and Valencia, and in April 2025 and May 2026 in multiple cities across Spain. Concurrent anti-tourism protests in 2024 and 2025 took place against the overcrowding of city centers and housing shortages that displace locals.


=== Scandals and incidents ===
A scandal broke out in early 2026 after it transpired that public housing in Alicante—a PP-ruled municipality—had been allocated to high-ranking party and city council officials (including the local official responsible for urban planning), their relatives, and friends. A judicial probe was opened to investigate possible crimes of malfeasance in office, insider trading, conflict of interest and political corruption.
Throughout the summer of 2026, it was revealed that the Madrid regional government had purchased a luxury penthouse valued at €6.3 million earlier that year; while the official purpose of the purchase remained unclear amid changing versions, it was suggested for use as a personal residence for regional premier Isabel Díaz Ayuso. The scandal inflamed public outrage amid the ongoing housing crisis, while legal proceedings were initiated regarding a possible misappropriation of public funds. During The District real estate fair in Madrid on 22 September 2026, three housing activists stormed the venue to protest against the policies of Ayuso, José Luis Martínez-Almeida (Madrid's mayor) and speculation, scattering leaflets and setting off stink bombs.
A 54-year-old woman from L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, Olga Matute, died by suicide in early September 2026 after being evicted from her home. Her eviction procedure had resumed after the Congress —with the votes of PP, Vox and Together for Catalonia (Junts)—struck down a decree-law in February 2026 extending a suspension of evictions approved by Sánchez's government in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.


== Developments ==


=== Maricarmen's eviction and initial protests ===

On 23 September, María del Carmen "Maricarmen" Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, was forcefully evicted from her home in Madrid after a long judicial struggle with a real estate company, Urbagestión. The case gained notoriety due to Maricarmen's vulnerable condition and Urbagestión's refusal to suspend the eviction despite pending court filings, humanitarian appeals, a volunteer's offer to cover her rent payments and attempts by public authorities to secure an alternative accommodation for her; as well as by the violent police response—seeing the use of tear gas—at protesters attempting to block the eviction, among whom were actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actress Ana Belén.
Maricarmen's case served as a catalyst for public discontent at the ongoing housing crisis in Spain, as well as a symbol for the pro-housing movement internationally. Following the eviction, a 10,000-strong spontaneous protest started in front of the Madrilenian government's luxury penthouse, with attendees calling for "Ayuso's penthouse for Maricarmen". The Madrid Tenants' Union (Spanish: Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid), which had organised eviction resistance in support of Maricarmen, called for a demonstration on 26 September which saw the participation of between 25,000 (according to authorities) and 300,000 people (according to organisers). This demonstration resulted in protesters spontaneously camping in the middle of the Puerta del Sol square, mirroring the 15-M Movement in 2011, to demand the Spanish government under Pedro Sánchez to ban evictions and push for stronger protection for tenants amid the housing shortage and soaring rents. Protests subsequently spread to other major Spanish cities, such as Valencia, Barcelona, Seville, Zaragoza, Málaga, Murcia, Vigo, A Coruña, Palma de Mallorca, Oviedo, Cádiz, Santiago de Compostela or Guadalajara.
On 29 September, the City Council of Madrid under Almeida demanded the immediate end of the Puerta del Sol camp, while the regional government in Madrid sent a formal request to the Spanish government to dismantle the camp within 48 hours or face legal action. These calls by PP-controlled administrations in Madrid came as Sánchez's government—formed by the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and Sumar—openly rejected forcefully clearing the encampment, and was joined by protests from campers that the clock chimes at the Royal House of the Post Office (Ayuso's headquarters as president of the Community of Madrid) rang every 15 minutes throughout the night and into the early morning, continuously interrupting their sleep. That same day, far-right groups such as Desokupa threatened on social media to storm Sol and evict the activists. By 30 September, the number of tents in Puerta del Sol had risen to over 1,200, with new encampments in support of the Madrid one spreading to major squares in cities such as Barcelona (Plaça de Catalunya) and Málaga (Plaza de la Constitución).


=== Government response and reactions ===

Mounting public pressure forced Urbagestión—the investment fund that had triggered Maricarmen's eviction—to backtrack and allow her to move back into the apartment, while prompting Sánchez's government to agree to emergency relief measures on housing. These measures, distributed in two decree-laws, included:

A ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030;
Bans on "vulture funds" buying property until 2028;
Regulation of temporary leases and room rentals;
A two-year extension on rental agreements due to expire before the end of 2028;
A VAT rate increase to 10% for tourist apartments, as well as a hike in the property tax (IBI) for such dwellings;
Zero-interest loans of up to €50,000 for the purchase of a first home ("Tu Casa" scheme);
Tax breaks for landlords and tenants to encourage a drop in rental prices;
A VAT rate reduction to 4% for housing construction;
Automatic renewal of rental agreements (with compensation of at least 12 months' rent if a landlord terminates a contract without just cause).

While tenant unions criticised the government's move to split the measures into two bills and regarded them as not ambitious enough, they also viewed them as a starting point and demanded their passage in parliament, calling for pressure actions on still-doubting parties. The Catalan government under Salvador Illa praised the central government's measures and announced an additional €125 million shared-ownership plan for families unable to secure a mortgage.
Sánchez's plans were dismissed by the right-wing opposition PP and Vox parties, with its approval relying on Junts's position. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo announced his party's outright opposition to the decrees even before the specific measures were unveiled, while Vox blamed the housing crisis on immigration and called for mass deportations. Republican Left of Catalonia, EH Bildu, Podemos, Més–Compromís and the Galician Nationalist Bloc all announced their support to the two bills, while the Basque Nationalist Party and Canarian Coalition announced their support for the first and their opposition to the second.
